mainTopic: Does a פועל eat from his own wages (משלו) or as a gift from Heaven (משל שמים)? Two ברייתות are tested against both sides.
overview: The גמרא is testing whether a worker who eats from the crop he works on eats 'from his own' (משלו, the food is part of his pay) or 'from Heaven' (משל שמים, a special gift the Torah gives him). First it finishes a ברייתא about tithes. That ברייתא seems to challenge משלו, but רבינא answers that the son's case only 'looks like a sale.' Next, a משנה about נטע רבעי seems to challenge משל שמים, and the גמרא answers that the hiring only 'looks like a mistaken deal.' The סיפא of that משנה, about opened wine barrels, seems to break this answer. The גמרא rescues it with two versions of when wine becomes obligated in מעשר, plus local customs that made the workers' mistake reasonable. Then a משנה about who may give up the right to eat is tested, and it is set against רבי הושעיא's ברייתא. The גמרא explains that the two do not argue: the difference is whether the man feeds his household, and a father may never make his young children suffer. The amud ends as the גמרא begins to challenge its reading of the משנה, and that challenge continues on the next amud.

steps.title: End of the ברייתא: the worker is exempt from tithes, his son is not
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא rules that a worker who eats is exempt from מעשר. If he arranged for his son to eat too, the son must tithe.
steps.simpleTranslation: This worker eats and does not need to separate מעשר. If he said 'on condition that my son and I eat' or 'that my son eats in place of my wages,' he himself eats without tithing, but his son must tithe before eating.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting a ברייתא it brought as a source for the question of whether a worker eats משלו or משל שמים. The ruling about the son is the part that the next step will use.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worker himself eats without tithing because the Torah gave him the right to eat while working. His son has no Torah right to eat, so the son's eating is treated like ordinary eating that needs מעשר. The question is how this fits each side of the debate.

keyTerms.meaning: Tithe, the portion that must be separated from produce before eating

phrases.aramaic: הֲרֵי זֶה אוֹכֵל וּפָטוּר מִן הַמַּעֲשֵׂר.
phrases.english: this one eats and is exempt from tithe.
phrases.notes: This is the end of a ברייתא that began just before, about a פועל who eats while working.

phrases.english: 'On condition that I and my son eat,'
or 'that my son eat in exchange for my wages'
he eats and is exempt,
and his son eats and is obligated.

steps.triggerLanguage: הֲרֵי זֶה אוֹכֵל וּפָטוּר מִן הַמַּעֲשֵׂר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a ברייתא that was brought before this section as a test of משלו or משל שמים.
steps.raayaObject: The question of whether a פועל eats משלו or משל שמים
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: the worker is exempt from מעשר, while his son is obligated

steps.title: Challenge: if the food is his own, why is the son obligated?
steps.stepSummary: If the worker eats from his own wages, the son should be exempt just like the father. Why is the son obligated?
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say the worker eats from his own, why is his son obligated to tithe?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses the ברייתא to attack the view that a worker eats משלו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the food is really the worker's own pay, then giving part of it to his son should work the same way as eating it himself, so the son should also be exempt. Since the ברייתא obligates the son, it seems the worker's right is a personal gift from Heaven that does not pass to others.

keyTerms.meaning: From his own (the food counts as his wages)

phrases.english: And if you say he eats from his own,
why is his son obligated?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a difficulty from the ברייתא in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that a פועל eats משלו
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the food is his own, his son eating in his place should be just as exempt. The son's obligation suggests the right is not really his property.

steps.title: רבינא: the son's case looks like a sale
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers that the son must tithe because the deal looks like a purchase, and bought produce needs מעשר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: it is because it looks like a sale.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא defends the view of משלו. The son's obligation is only because of how the deal looks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By the letter of the law the food is the worker's, so the son could have been exempt. But when the father trades his wages for food for his son, it looks like buying produce, and bought produce requires מעשר. The rule about the son therefore does not disprove משלו.
steps.confusionAlert: רבינא is not saying it really is a sale. It only looks like one, so חכמים required מעשר.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
Because it looks like a sale.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reason reassignment: the son's obligation comes from appearance, not from the nature of the worker's right.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The son's obligation proves the food is not the worker's own.
steps.terutzMaskana: The food may still be the worker's own. The son must tithe only because the arrangement looks like a sale.

steps.title: New source: workers hired for נטע רבעי
steps.stepSummary: A משנה: workers on fourth-year fruit may not eat it. If the owner did not tell them, he must redeem the fruit and feed them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: one who hires a worker to work with his fourth-year fruit — they may not eat. If he did not tell them, he redeems the fruit and lets them eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new משנה to test the question again. This step sets up the challenge that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נטע רבעי is holy and may not be eaten freely, so the workers cannot eat it. The surprising part is the second ruling: if the owner kept it from them, he must pay to redeem the fruit so they can eat. That obligation is what the גמרא will examine.

keyTerms.meaning: Fruit of a tree's fourth year, which must be eaten in ירושלים or redeemed
He redeems, moving the holiness onto money

phrases.english: Come and hear:
One who hires the worker
to work with his fourth-year fruit
these may not eat.
And if he did not inform them,
he redeems and feeds them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 3 deflected the first proof, a second source is brought.
steps.raayaObject: The question of whether a פועל eats משלו or משל שמים
steps.raayaSupportSource: A משנה (on 93a) about workers on נטע רבעי

steps.title: Challenge: if it is Heaven's gift, why must the owner feed them?
steps.stepSummary: If the worker's eating is a gift from Heaven, the Torah never gave him forbidden food, so why must the owner redeem and feed?
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say he eats from Heaven's, why does the owner redeem and feed them? The Torah does not grant them something forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא uses the רבעי משנה to attack the view of משל שמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If eating is only a Torah gift, that gift covers permitted food, not forbidden רבעי. So the workers never had any right here, and the owner should owe nothing. Since he must redeem and feed them, it seems the food is part of their wages, which is משלו.

keyTerms.meaning: From Heaven's, a gift the Torah grants
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אָמְרַתְּ מִשֶּׁל שָׁמַיִם הוּא אוֹכֵל –
phrases.english: And if you say he eats from Heaven's,
why does he redeem and feed them?
The Merciful One did not grant them something forbidden!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אָמְרַתְּ מִשֶּׁל שָׁמַיִם הוּא אוֹכֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a difficulty from the משנה in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that a פועל eats משל שמים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A Heavenly gift would not cover forbidden food, so the owner should owe nothing. Requiring him to redeem and feed suggests the food is the worker's wages.

steps.title: Answer: it looks like a mistaken deal
steps.stepSummary: The owner must feed them only because the hiring looks like a deal made under false assumptions.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it is because it looks like a mistaken deal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the view of משל שמים by giving a different reason why the owner must feed the workers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The workers took the job expecting to eat, and the owner hid that the fruit was רבעי. That makes the hiring look like a deal based on a mistake, so he must make it up to them. The obligation comes from how he misled them, not from a wage right in the fruit.

keyTerms.meaning: A mistaken deal, a transaction made under a false assumption

steps.whatToRemember: Both proofs were turned aside with a 'looks like' reason: the son's case looks like a sale, and the רבעי case looks like a mistaken deal. Neither proof settles the question, so the גמרא brings more sources in the next steps.

phrases.english: There, it is because it looks like a mistaken deal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reason reassignment: the duty to feed comes from the misleading hiring, not from a wage right.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The owner's duty to feed proves the food is the workers' own wages.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even if eating is משל שמים, the owner must compensate because the hiring looks like a מקח טעות.

steps.title: The end of the teaching: broken fig cakes and opened barrels
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the end of the same teaching. Workers fixing broken fig cakes or opened wine barrels may not eat, but if they were not told, the owner must tithe the food and feed them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Look at the end of the teaching: if his fig cakes broke apart or his barrels opened, the workers he hires may not eat. If he did not tell them, he must tithe the food and feed them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new piece of evidence from the end of the same teaching it quoted in step 4. It is setting up a new challenge in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once figs are pressed into cakes and wine is in barrels, the food is already obligated in מעשר, so a worker cannot eat from it. Even so, if the owner did not warn the workers, he must tithe the food and feed them. That rule will be used to show where the worker's right to eat comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: Say the latter part (of the teaching)
His pressed fig cakes broke apart
He tithes the food and feeds them

phrases.english: Say the latter clause:
phrases.notes: This is the end of the same teaching about fourth-year fruit quoted in step 4.

phrases.english: If his fig cakes broke apart,
or his barrels opened,
these workers may not eat,
and if he did not inform them,
he tithes and feeds them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first proof in steps 4 to 6 was answered, the גמרא brings a second proof from the same teaching.
steps.raayaObject: Whether the worker eats משלו (from his own, as wages) or משל שמים (as a gift from Heaven).
steps.raayaSupportSource: The end of the teaching about workers and fourth-year fruit: the owner must tithe the food and feed workers he did not warn.

steps.title: If the eating comes from Heaven, why tithe and feed them?
steps.stepSummary: If the worker eats from Heaven's property, the Torah never gave him forbidden food, so the owner should not have to tithe it and feed him.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say the worker eats from Heaven's property, why must the owner tithe the food and feed them? The Torah never gave them a right to forbidden food!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns the case into a challenge against the view that the worker eats 'from Heaven'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the Torah is the one giving the worker his food, it never gave him untithed food, so he has no claim at all. The fact that the owner must fix the food and feed him suggests the worker eats from what the owner owes him. This is the same kind of question as step 5, now asked about a new case.

keyTerms.meaning: From Heaven's property, a gift of the Torah

phrases.english: But if you say
he eats from what belongs to Heaven,
why must he tithe and feed them?
The Merciful One did not give them a right to forbidden food!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אָמְרַתְּ מִשֶּׁל שָׁמַיִם הוּא אוֹכֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the challenge out of the case quoted in step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that a worker eats 'from Heaven'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A Torah gift would never include forbidden food, so the owner's duty to tithe and feed must come from his own obligation to the worker.

steps.title: The mistaken-deal answer works for fig cakes but not for wine
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא considers the earlier answer, that it looks like a מקח טעות. That answer fits the broken fig cakes, but not the opened barrels, because the workers know wine is already obligated in מעשר.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you will say that here too it is because it looks like a mistaken deal: that works when his fig cakes broke apart. But when his barrels opened, what mistaken deal is there? They surely know the wine is already obligated in tithes!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to reuse the answer from step 6 and shows that it does not work for the wine barrels.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the fig cakes, the workers could think the figs had not yet been pressed, so they did not know the figs were obligated. That is a real misunderstanding. With wine in barrels, everyone knows it is already obligated, so the workers were not fooled and the answer from step 6 seems to fail. The next step answers this.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you will say (a suggested answer)
A deal made under a mistaken assumption
It became obligated in tithes (it became טבל)

phrases.english: And if you will say:
here too
it is because it looks like a mistaken deal.
Granted, when his fig cakes broke apart,
it looks like a mistaken deal.
But when his barrels opened,
what mistaken deal is there?
They surely know
that it already became obligated in tithes!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Blocks the expected defense against step 8 by showing that the step 6 answer does not fit the barrels case.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The use of the מקח טעות answer for the case of the opened barrels.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Wine in barrels is clearly obligated in tithes, so the workers could not have been misled.

steps.title: רב ששת: the barrels spilled back into the pit
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת explains that the barrels opened and the wine spilled back into the pit, so the workers could think it was not yet obligated.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: the case is that his barrels opened into the pit.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת rescues the מקח טעות answer by describing the barrels case in a specific way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the wine poured back into the pit near the winepress, the workers could think it was at an early stage and not yet obligated. Then there is a real misunderstanding, just like with the fig cakes.

keyTerms.meaning: The pit next to the winepress where the juice collects

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said:
The case is that his barrels opened into the pit.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת שֶׁנִּתְפַּתְּחוּ חָבִיּוֹתָיו לַבּוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 9 by narrowing the case so that a misunderstanding is possible.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Wine in barrels is clearly obligated, so the workers could not have been misled.
steps.terutzMaskana: The wine fell back into the pit, so the workers could think it was not yet obligated.

steps.title: But wine is obligated once it goes into the pit
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that wine is obligated in מעשר from the moment it goes down into the pit, so falling into the pit should not mislead anyone.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is taught: wine becomes obligated from when it goes down into the pit!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב ששת with a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If wine is already obligated once it reaches the pit, then wine lying in the pit is clearly obligated. The workers still could not think it was exempt, so רב ששת's answer seems to fail.

phrases.english: But isn't it taught:
wine is obligated from when it goes down into the pit!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב ששת's answer in step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's claim that wine in the pit could seem exempt.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא says wine is obligated as soon as it reaches the pit, so there is no room for a mistake.

steps.title: Following רבי עקיבא: wine is obligated only once skimmed
steps.stepSummary: The teaching follows רבי עקיבא, who says wine becomes obligated only once it is skimmed. The workers can say they did not know it had been skimmed.
steps.simpleTranslation: It follows רבי עקיבא, who says wine is obligated from when it is skimmed. That is why the workers can say to the owner, 'We did not know.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by saying the teaching follows a different opinion about when wine becomes obligated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי עקיבא, wine in the pit is not obligated until the seeds and skins that float to the top are skimmed off. The workers did not know the skimming had already been done, so they thought the wine was still exempt. That brings back a real misunderstanding.

keyTerms.meaning: Skims off the seeds and skins floating on top

phrases.english: It follows Rabbi Akiva,
who says: from when he skims it,
for they can say to him:
We did not know.
phrases.notes: They mean they did not know the wine had already been skimmed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 11 by tying the teaching to רבי עקיבא's opinion.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Wine is obligated as soon as it is in the pit, so no one could be misled.
steps.terutzMaskana: According to רבי עקיבא, it is obligated only after skimming, which the workers did not know about.

steps.title: They should have suspected it was skimmed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: the workers should have thought that the wine might already have been skimmed.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us tell them: you should have thought that maybe he already skimmed it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the workers' excuse of 'we did not know'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A misunderstanding only counts if it was reasonable. If the workers should have suspected the skimming was done, their mistake is their own fault, and the owner would not have to feed them.

keyTerms.meaning: To bring up in your minds, to consider

phrases.english: But let us say to them:
You should have considered in your minds
that perhaps he had already skimmed it!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְנֵימָא לְהוּ אִיבְּעִי לְכוּ אַסּוֹקֵי אַדַּעְתַּיְיכוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether the workers' claim in step 12 is reasonable.
steps.kashyaTarget: The workers' claim that they did not know.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: They should have thought of the possibility that the wine was skimmed, so their mistake should not count.

steps.title: Where the one who draws the wine also skims it
steps.stepSummary: The case is in a place where the same person who draws the wine also skims it, so the workers could fairly assume the skimming had not been done.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is in a place where the same man who draws the wine is the one who skims it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the workers' mistake by describing local practice, and this closes this round of questions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Where drawing and skimming are done by the same worker, workers hired to handle the wine would naturally think the skimming was part of their own job. That means it was not done yet, so the wine was not yet obligated. Their mistake was reasonable, so the 'mistaken deal' answer from step 6 works for the barrels too, and the challenge from step 8 against משל שמים is answered.

keyTerms.meaning: A place, a locality with its own custom
Draws or pulls the wine out

steps.whatToRemember: The owner must feed workers he did not warn only when their mistake was reasonable. That is why the גמרא works so hard to show how the workers could honestly think the wine was still exempt.

phrases.english: In a place where that same man
who draws the wine is the one who skims it!

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּאַתְרָא דְּהָהוּא גַּבְרָא דְּנָגֵיד אִיהוּ מְקַפֶּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 13 by showing why the workers' assumption was reasonable.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case to a local practice
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The workers should have suspected the wine was skimmed.
steps.terutzMaskana: Where the one who draws the wine also skims it, workers would fairly think the skimming had not been done.

steps.title: A different version of the dispute gives a simpler answer
steps.stepSummary: Based on רב זביד's version, where רבי עקיבא says wine is obligated only once the waste is drained from the barrels, the workers' mistake works even if the barrels never opened back into the pit.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now that רב זביד taught from the school of רבי הושעיא, 'Wine is obligated from when it goes down into the pit and the waste floats up, and רבי עקיבא says: from when he drains the waste from the barrels,' you can even say the barrels did not spill back into the pit. The workers could say: 'We did not know he had already drained it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a new, easier way to explain the wine story, based on a different version of the dispute about when wine becomes obligated in מעשר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, רב ששת needed the wine to spill back into the pit to explain the workers' mistake. In רב זביד's version, רבי עקיבא puts the moment of obligation even later, when the waste is drained in the barrels. So the barrels only need to have been opened, and the workers can say they did not know the draining was done.

keyTerms.meaning: From the study hall (school) of רבי הושעיא
And the waste floats up to the top (so it can be skimmed)
From when he drains off (removes) the waste

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix the two versions. In the earlier version, רבי עקיבא's moment was the skimming. In רב זביד's version, רבי עקיבא's moment is the draining in the barrels, and the skimming at the pit belongs to the first opinion.

phrases.aramaic: וְהַשְׁתָּא דְּתָנֵי רַב זְבִיד בִּדְבֵי רַבִּי הוֹשַׁעְיָא:
phrases.english: And now that Rav Zevid taught from the school of Rabbi Hoshaya:
Wine is obligated from when it goes down into the pit and its waste floats up,
and Rabbi Akiva says: from when he drains the waste in the barrels.

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא שֶׁלֹּא נִתְפַּתְּחוּ חָבִיּוֹתָיו לַבּוֹר,
phrases.english: You can even say that his barrels did not burst open into the pit,

phrases.aramaic: דַּאֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ: לָא הֲוָה יָדְעִינַן דִּמְשַׁלֵּי.
phrases.english: because they can say to him: We did not know that he had drained it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second, simpler explanation of the same wine story, based on a different version of the dispute.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different version of the underlying ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We needed the barrels to spill back into the pit to explain why the workers thought the wine was not yet obligated.
steps.terutzMaskana: With רבי עקיבא's later moment of obligation (draining in the barrels), the workers can simply say they did not know the draining had happened.

steps.title: They should have suspected it was already drained
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the new answer: the workers should have considered that the waste might already have been drained.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us say to them: You should have thought that maybe it was already drained!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks the same kind of question it asked before, now aimed at the new version: the workers should have been more careful.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An honest mistake only works if the workers had no reason to suspect anything. If draining is something that might already have happened, they should have taken that into account. So their claim of not knowing seems weak.

keyTerms.meaning: To bring it up in your minds, to think of it

phrases.english: But let us say to them:
You should have brought it into your minds
that maybe it was already drained!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the new answer in step 15, the same way step 13 attacked the earlier answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the workers honestly did not know the wine had been drained.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Reasonable workers should have suspected the draining might have been done, so they cannot claim innocence.

steps.title: Where the same person seals and drains the barrels
steps.stepSummary: The case is in a place where the man who seals the barrels is also the one who drains them, so the workers fairly assumed the draining had not been done yet.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is in a place where the same person who seals the barrel is the one who drains it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by describing a local custom that made the workers' assumption reasonable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this place, sealing and draining are done by the same worker. Since these workers were hired for the job, they assumed the draining was still part of their work and had not happened yet. So their mistake was understandable.

keyTerms.meaning: In a place (where the custom is)

phrases.english: In a place where the one who seals the barrel
is the same one who drains it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16 with a local custom, just as step 14 answered step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case to a specific local custom
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The workers had no excuse, since the draining might have been done already.
steps.terutzMaskana: Where the sealer is also the drainer, the workers reasonably assumed the draining was still their job and had not been done.
steps.whatToRemember: With either version of the dispute, the wine story can be explained as an honest mistake by the workers. Each version comes with its own question and answer.

steps.title: A new proof: who can waive the right to eat
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה: a man may give up the right to eat for himself and the adults in his household, but not for minors or his animal, because they lack understanding.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: A man may arrange to give up eating, in return for higher pay, for himself, for his adult son and daughter, for his adult slave and maidservant, and for his wife, because they have understanding. But he may not do this for his minor son and daughter, for his minor slave and maidservant, or for his animal, because they do not have understanding.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source to help settle whether a worker eats משל שמים or משלו. This step only quotes the משנה; the next step will show how it proves the point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says adults can give up their right to eat, but minors and animals cannot. The reason it gives is דעת, the ability to understand and agree. The גמרא will now ask what this rule tells us about the nature of the worker's right to eat.

keyTerms.meaning: Arranges ahead of time (to give up eating in exchange for more pay)

phrases.english: Come and hear:
A man may make an arrangement for himself,
phrases.notes: He means arranging extra pay in place of eating the produce while working.

phrases.english: for his adult son and daughter,
for his adult slave and maidservant,
and for his wife,
because they have understanding.
But he may not make this arrangement

phrases.aramaic: לֹא עַל יְדֵי בְּנוֹ וּבִתּוֹ הַקְּטַנִּים,
phrases.english: not for his minor son and daughter,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא עַל יְדֵי עַבְדּוֹ וְשִׁפְחָתוֹ הַקְּטַנִּים,
phrases.english: nor for his minor slave and maidservant,
nor for his animal,
because they do not have understanding.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: קוֹצֵץ אָדָם עַל יְדֵי עַצְמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the wine story and brings a new source for the main question of משל שמים versus משלו.
steps.raayaObject: Whether a worker eats משל שמים or משלו.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A משנה (on 93a) about who may give up the right to eat while working.

steps.title: Why minors cannot give up eating
steps.stepSummary: Assuming the man feeds his household, the rule about minors makes sense if a worker eats משל שמים, but not if he eats משלו.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might think this is a case where he feeds them. It works well if you say a worker eats משל שמים; that is why he cannot arrange it for minors. But if you say he eats משלו, he should be able to arrange it for minors too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how the משנה proves its point, and turns it into a challenge against the view that a worker eats משלו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: We assume the father or master feeds these people, so their work earnings belong to him. If eating is a gift from the Torah (משל שמים), it belongs to the minor himself, and a minor cannot give it up. But if eating is part of the wages (משלו), the wages already belong to the provider, so he should be able to trade them away even for minors.

keyTerms.meaning: Where he provides them with food
From what belongs to Heaven, a right granted by the Torah
From his own, as part of his wages
It works well if you say

steps.confusionAlert: The words 'קא סלקא דעתך' signal that this is only a first assumption (that he feeds them). In step 20 the גמרא rejects this assumption and explains the משנה differently.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a real test case for the main question. The difference between משל שמים and משלו decides who owns the right to eat, and so who can give it up.

phrases.english: It enters your mind
that he provides them with food.
It works well if you say
that he eats from what belongs to Heaven,
that is why he cannot make the arrangement for minors,
but if you say
that he eats from his own wages,
let him make the arrangement for minors too!

steps.triggerLanguage: קָא סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ בְּמַעֲלֶה לָהֶן מְזוֹנוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the משנה quoted in step 18.
steps.raayaObject: That a worker eats משל שמים.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's rule that a man cannot give up the right to eat for minors, read as a case where he feeds them.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that a worker eats משלו.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If eating is part of the wages, and the wages belong to the provider who feeds them, he should be able to give up eating even for minors.

steps.title: The משנה is about a man who does not feed them
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof from step 19 by placing the משנה in a case where the man does not provide food for his household.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here we are dealing with a case where he does not provide them with food.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof that a worker eats משל שמים. It says the משנה is talking about a man who does not feed his household.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 19 assumed the man feeds his household, so their earnings and food rights would belong to him. If he does not feed them, their food rights are not his to give away. So even if a worker eats משלו, he cannot waive the rights of minors.

keyTerms.meaning: With what are we dealing here? (a phrase that limits a source to a specific case)

phrases.english: Here, with what are we dealing?
When he does not provide them with food.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 19 by changing its assumed case.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The assumption in step 19 that the man feeds his household.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof only works if he feeds them; the משנה can be read as a case where he does not.

steps.title: Then adults should be the same
steps.stepSummary: If he does not feed them, he should not be able to give up the rights of his adult household members either.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, adults too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new reading. If he does not feed them, why may he give up eating rights for adults?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה allows waiving for adults. But if he does not feed the adults either, their food rights are not his. So the new reading seems to break the משנה's rule about adults.

phrases.english: If so,
adults too!
phrases.notes: He means: then he shouldn't be able to give up eating rights for the adults either.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the case setting proposed in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the משנה speaks of a man who does not feed his household.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If he does not feed them, he has no right to give up anyone's food, adults included, yet the משנה lets him do it for adults.

steps.title: Adults know and agree to give it up
steps.stepSummary: Adults understand the deal and agree to give up their right to eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: Adults know and they forgive.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that adults are aware of the arrangement and willingly give up their right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The father is not really waiving the adults' rights for them. The adults agree themselves. Minors cannot agree, because they lack understanding, so he cannot do it for them.

keyTerms.meaning: They forgive or give up a right

phrases.english: Adults know
and they forgive.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction between adults and minors based on their ability to agree
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The father waives for everyone, so adults and minors should be treated the same.
steps.terutzMaskana: Adults give up the right themselves; minors cannot, so the father cannot do it for them.

steps.title: A ברייתא allows it for minor slaves
steps.stepSummary: רבי הושעיא's ברייתא says a man may give up eating rights for his Canaanite slaves, even minors, which seems to contradict the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't רבי הושעיא teach: A person may stipulate for himself and his wife, but not for his animal; for his adult son and daughter, but not for his minor son and daughter; and he may stipulate for his Canaanite slave and maidservant, whether adults or minors.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that lets a man give up eating rights even for his minor slaves. This clashes with the משנה, which does not allow it for minors.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says minors cannot be included because they lack understanding. The ברייתא agrees about minor children but allows it for minor slaves. So the two sources seem to disagree about minor slaves.

keyTerms.meaning: Stipulates (agrees to more pay instead of eating)

phrases.english: But didn't Rabbi Hoshaya teach:
A person may stipulate on his own behalf
phrases.notes: Stipulate here means agreeing to extra pay instead of eating the produce while working.

phrases.english: and on his wife's behalf,
but not on behalf of his animal.
And on behalf of his adult son and daughter,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל לֹא עַל יְדֵי בְּנוֹ וּבִתּוֹ הַקְּטַנִּים.
phrases.english: but not on behalf of his minor son and daughter.

phrases.aramaic: וְקוֹצֵץ עַל יְדֵי עַבְדּוֹ וְשִׁפְחָתוֹ הַכְּנַעֲנִים,
phrases.english: And he may stipulate on behalf of his Canaanite slave and maidservant,
whether adults or minors.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises a contradiction between the משנה of step 18 and a ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule that one cannot stipulate for minors.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא allows stipulating for minor slaves, directly against the משנה.

steps.title: Maybe they argue about משלו versus משל שמים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests both sources speak of a man who feeds his slaves, and they disagree about whether a worker eats משלו or משל שמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't it that both speak of where he provides them with food, and they disagree on this: one Sage holds a worker eats from his own, and one Sage holds he eats from Heaven's?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests a way to explain the clash: the משנה and the ברייתא disagree about the basic nature of a worker's eating right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a worker eats משלו, the right is part of his earnings, which belong to the master, so the master can waive it (the ברייתא). If he eats משל שמים, it is Heaven's gift to the worker himself, and a minor cannot give it up (the משנה, as in step 19). This would prove there is a real dispute on the question.

keyTerms.meaning: What, is it not that (introduces a suggested reading)
This one and that one, both
From Heaven's (a gift from the Torah)

phrases.english: What, is it not that
both this and that are where he provides them with food,
and they disagree about this:
one Sage holds he eats from his own,

phrases.aramaic: וּמָר סָבַר מִשֶּׁל שָׁמַיִם הוּא אוֹכֵל?!
phrases.english: and one Sage holds he eats from Heaven's?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי לָאו, אִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי בְּמַעֲלֶה לָהֶן מְזוֹנוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction of step 23 by turning it into a dispute.
steps.raayaObject: That the משלו versus משל שמים question is a real dispute between תנאים.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The contradiction between the משנה and רבי הושעיא's ברייתא.

steps.title: Everyone holds משלו; the cases are different
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion: all agree a worker eats משלו, and the משנה speaks of not feeding them while the ברייתא speaks of feeding them.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, everyone agrees he eats from his own, and it is not difficult: here, when he does not provide them with food; the ברייתא, when he provides them with food.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says there is no dispute at all. The two sources simply describe two different cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה he does not feed his minor slaves, so their food rights are not his, and they cannot waive them themselves. In the ברייתא he feeds them, so their earnings are his, and he can waive. Both fit the view that a worker eats משלו.

keyTerms.meaning: A teaching from the time of the משנה not included in it

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה and the ברייתא do not argue. Both hold a worker eats משלו; the difference is whether the master feeds the slaves.

phrases.english: No,
everyone agrees he eats from his own,
and it is not difficult:
here, when he does not provide them with food,
phrases.notes: Here means the משנה, as explained back in step 20.

phrases.english: and the ברייתא, when he provides them with food.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא מִשֶּׁלּוֹ הוּא אוֹכֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the dispute suggested in step 24.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The claim that the sources disagree about משלו versus משל שמים.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The contradiction can be solved by placing each source in a different case, with no dispute needed.

steps.title: Then he should be able to do it for minor children
steps.stepSummary: If the ברייתא speaks of a man who feeds them, he should also be able to waive for his minor children, yet the ברייתא forbids it.
steps.simpleTranslation: How did you explain the ברייתא? Where he provides them with food? If so, let him stipulate for minors too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new reading of the ברייתא. If he feeds everyone, why can he not waive for his minor children, the way he can for minor slaves?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reason given for minor slaves is that he feeds them, so their earnings belong to him. A father who feeds his young children should be in the same position. Yet the ברייתא says he cannot stipulate for them.

keyTerms.meaning: How did you set up (explain) it?

phrases.english: How did you set it up?
Where he provides them with food?
If so,
let him stipulate for the minors too!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reading of the ברייתא given in step 25.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that the ברייתא speaks of a man who feeds his household.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If feeding them makes their earnings his, it should work for minor children just as for minor slaves.

steps.title: The Torah does not let him make his young children suffer
steps.stepSummary: A father may not waive his minor children's eating rights because the Torah does not give him the right to cause them suffering.
steps.simpleTranslation: The suffering of his minor son and daughter, the Merciful One did not grant to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that minor children are different: the Torah does not let a father cause them the pain of seeing food and not eating it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though he feeds them and their earnings are his, a small child working near food will suffer if not allowed to eat. The Torah does not give the father control over that suffering. Slaves are not included in this special protection, so for them the stipulation works.
steps.whatToRemember: A father who feeds his family can waive eating rights for minor slaves but never for his own minor children, because the Torah does not let him cause them that suffering.

phrases.english: The suffering of his minor son and daughter
the Merciful One did not grant to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: צַעֲרַיְיהוּ דִּבְנוֹ וּבִתּוֹ הַקְּטַנִּים לָא זַכִּי לֵיהּ רַחֲמָנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A special reason that applies only to minor children
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since he feeds them, he could waive for minor children just as for minor slaves.
steps.terutzMaskana: The Torah does not give a father control over his young children's suffering, so he cannot waive for them.

steps.title: Recalling how the משנה was explained, to prepare a new challenge
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא restates its earlier explanation: the משנה speaks of a man who does not provide food for his slaves. This sets up a challenge against that explanation.
steps.simpleTranslation: How did you explain our משנה? As speaking of a case where he does not provide them with food.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is reminding us how it explained the משנה in Step 25: the owner does not feed his slaves. This line only sets up the next move, a challenge that will test whether this explanation really works.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In steps 20 and 25 the גמרא said the משנה forbids giving up the minors' eating rights because the owner does not feed them. Here the גמרא brings that explanation back on purpose. The challenge to it continues on the next amud, so the learner should keep this explanation in mind as the thing being tested.

keyTerms.meaning: How did you explain it? Literally, 'in what case did you set it up?'
He provides them with food (supports them)

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not a new ruling. It only repeats the explanation from Step 25 so the גמרא can challenge it right after.

phrases.english: In what case did you explain our משנה?
phrases.notes: This points back to Step 25, where the גמרא explained what case the משנה is talking about.

phrases.english: As a case where he does not provide them with food,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Steps 26-27 dealt with a challenge against the ברייתא. This step returns to the explanation of the משנה from Step 25, so it can be challenged next.
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation from Step 25 that the משנה speaks of an owner who does not feed his slaves.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Restating the explanation sets up a test. The גמרא will check whether 'he does not feed them' fits the rest of the משנה's wording.
